messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 20
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Doctor
- Trauma Type: Combat
- Pcl5: 63

The dust still tastes like copper and burnt diesel to him, though he has been away from the theater for eight months. He is twenty now, but in the memory that wakes him at 3:14 a.m., he is eighteen again, crouched behind a collapsed wall as the sky cracks open. He remembers the weight of his rifle, the sudden silence before the first mortar falls, and the way his comrade’s name dissolves into the chaos. He survived the extraction, but something inside him did not. Now, he sits on the edge of the examination table in my office, fingers tracing the seam of his scrub top, while the morning light filters through the blinds. Medical school does not offer him the clean break he had hoped for. He has always believed that healing the body will quiet the mind, and so he trades combat fatigues for white coats, moving through lecture halls with the same rigid posture he still carries in the hospital wards. He works now as a first-year physician on a busy urban emergency department, one of the youngest in his cohort. His colleagues admire his steady hands and his uncanny ability to remain calm when alarms blare, but they do not know that his calm is a held breath. Every triage screen feels like a checkpoint. Every sudden code blue sends a jolt down his spine that no amount of procedural repetition can erase. He double-checks IV lines three times. He memorizes dosages by heart. He tells himself it is just thoroughness, but the exhaustion is a constant hum beneath his ribs. His family’s West African roots have always grounded him in a culture that views endurance as a quiet virtue, yet nothing in his upbringing prepared him for the silence that follows gunfire. He avoids the subway after his shift, walking the extra six blocks home because the rumble of the train feels too much like distant artillery. His apartment is sparse, the furniture arranged so that the door and windows are never behind him. He dreams of the wall, of the silence, of the way his own hands look when they cannot stop the bleeding. When he wakes, his heart hammers against his sternum, and for a moment, he does not know where he is. In therapy, he speaks in careful, measured sentences, but his eyes keep tracking the clock, the exit, the shadow falling across the rug. He describes the guilt as a stone in his throat. He admits he has stopped calling his parents because their voices make him ache with a longing he cannot name. He is single, not by choice, but because intimacy requires a softness he feels he no longer possesses. Today, he leans forward, elbows on his knees, and watches his own hands. “I saved so many people this week,” he says, voice low. “I pulled a man back from the edge of cardiac arrest. I sutured a laceration on a child’s cheek without her crying. And tonight, I sat in my kitchen and stared at the microwave because it beeped too loudly.” He exhales, long and slow, as if letting go of something heavy. The room is quiet. He does not look at the door. He does not look away from his hands. He simply waits, breathing in the familiar scent of old paper and wood, carrying the weight of two lives—one he left behind in the dust, and one he is still learning how to hold.
